Establishing Safety and Beginning Integration In the example above, the spiritual director lielped the spiritual directee feel safe and begin to integrate her expe- riences more fully into her spiritual journey. Establishing safery and beginning integration constitute the first stage of working with a spiritual directee who has PTSD, espe- cially one who is a fledgling in explicitly bringing such experiences to God. We can see the dynamics of this first stage as we look more closely at the example. The spiritual directee described the "triggering" of her symptoms as "intrusions" that threatened to interfère with her prayer, yet she expressed hope for healing. She trusted her spiritual director and felt safe enough to reveal what was happening. The spiritual director responded with calm support, acceprance, and engagement, yet without pressing for details. To press for details is to risk re-traumatizing the spiritual directee. "Intrusions" occur in persons with PTSD because Co hen unknown to them) they are actually trying to integrate experiences that are extraordinarily difficult to integrate. The spiritual directee's hope for healing (no doubt God's desire, too) was thereby explicitly supported. The spiritual director conveyed that it was safe and appropriate to speak to her and to God about these struggles. The door was opened for the spiri- tual directee to continue te, speak about them during the retreat. Keeping the spiritual directee in the rhythm and structure of the retreat reinforced saféty and normaliry. The reminder about telephone numbers was a very prac- tical way to provide saféty. The spiritual directee had, but did not recall, trau - matic nightmares—another common feature of PTSD. These are not usuel dreams; they are recurring intrusions of buried memories. Ironically, the senne of safety in spiritual direction ma t' increase the likelihood of such memories coming to consciousness. In this case, the lack of recall suggested that the spiritual directee coula not yet tolerate remembering all the deuils of her trauma. The spiritual director wisely did not probe the nightmare. If a spiritual directee remembers a nightmare and speaks about it, the spiritual director can respond as with other difficult information. The spiritual director can express empathy and encourage the spiritual directee's own judg- ment about writing it down, processing it, or consulting a counselor. The spiritual director also promoted integration by focusing on the spiritual directee's feeling of fear as important to pray about. Not only was the spiritual directee supported by the spiritual director as she faced her fears, in prayer she Pound her- self in the Company of Mary and Jacob and God. Her hypervigi - lance transformed into a prayerful vigil, during which she was reas- sured by God. Facing her fears in prayer reduced their potency, brought freedom, and opened the experience to further revelation as well as potentiel healing. God responded to the spiritual directee and brought her reassurance and healing. Spiritual directors can help in exploring these. Many persons have difficulry getting the events of their trauma into a coherent foret and articulating what hap - pened. They have only fragments of information with which to work and buried memories that trouble them. Now I realize God isn't that way. » Piecing Together and Telling the Story Unlike the first example, the spiritual director in this story did not know the spiritual directee had PTSD. As a child the spiritual directee witnessed the death and seri- ons injury of loved ones. She now had trouble recalling détails, usually avoided speaking about what happened, experienced flashback, struggled with a désire for con - trol, had grief over what happened or failed tc, happen long ago, and was significantly affected in other ways by the trauma, including how she saw herself in relation to others and God. All of these are characteristic of persons with PTSD, but because the spiritual directee did not mention having the diagnoses, there was no certainty. Possibly the spiritual directee herself did nos know. Such uncertainty will often be the case in spiri- tual direction. Knowing that the trauma happened and that there were lingering effects neverthe- less allowed the spiritual director to be thoughtful about how to proceed. The example illustrates piccing together and telling the story, the second stage encountered by spiritual directees with PTSD (or characteristics similar to it) and their spiritual directors. First the spiritual director helped establish safery and the beginning of intégration. The spiritual directee expe- rienced God's peace in prayer, but then the unpeaceful came to light'. The spiritual director did not probe the story but simply let the spiritual directee go at her own pace. A new loss opened up grief over an old loss, and God invited engagement with chat. The spiritual directee gradually surrendered her reluctance and aligned with God in gathering the pieces of her story. The spiritual director and the spiritual directee trusted God to bring-the pieces when the spiritual directee could handle them. Olten what is deeply concealed must be slowly dis - closed, as happened in this exemple. Organiz ing the pieces of one's story reduces both the sense of chaos about a trauma and the continuai desire for control in one's lite. When the spiritual directee gave over control to God, she relived a very difficult part of the story in a flashback. For a narrative to be healing, confronting such concrete and explicit details is frequently required and demands courage. Scories are ways to face such things and to come to terras with feelings about them, as was truc for this spiritual directee. Her feelings of gratitude and compas- sion began to flow, even in the context of horror. The spiritual director offered prayer suggestions appropriate to the spiritual directee's emotional stase and reminded her of mental health support options. Finally, ail the hid- den pieces seemed to have come to light, and the spiritual directee could tell her complete story. The spiritual director witnessed, affirmed, showed interest and empathy, encouraged, supported, compan - ioned, noticed, and listened to the spiritual direct ee throughout the piecing together and telling of her story. In piecing her story together and telling it, the spiritual directee made it available to herself and to her spiritual director. Through her story she gradually appreciated her own strength of character and grew in relationship with God. Her story connected te, the larget story of who she and her mother became and what God desires for her. Human beings tell stories for these reasons; they wish to say something about who they are and to declare that their experience is more chan a sequence of events. Although she did not sec God per se in the story, the spiritual directee felt God's help in her remembering, and she modified her image of God. It may cake a very long time for spiritual directees with PTSD te, be able to tell their complete stories. This stage may involve numerous iterations as new and even surprising fragments come to light. All are opportunities for deeper freedom, integration, and growth in relation - ship with God. These are what keep the spiritual directee going. God calls forth the storytelling of persons with PTSD and sustains them in courage to bring them heal - ing. The spiritual directee who feels safe and is trying to piece the story together may tell or write or draw the story again and again until a missing piece cornes and the story is revised to accommodate it. Frequent returns tc, the past seem counter to the popular notion of staying in the present moment, yet it is essentiel for integration and healing that the spiritual directee respond to the compel- ling grace at work. It is a process the scripture writers would have recognized. These are visits, not dwelling places. God sustains the listening spiritual director in patience, understanding, and compassion, out of love for both spiritual director and spiritual directee as they construct a new exodus story together. Once a spiritual directee has a coherent story about a trauma, it may still cake time to Find God in the story. In fast, God may be consciously or unconsciously blamed for what happened orbe seen as a big disappointment for failing to help. Eventually, God's role must be confronted by the spiritual directee for the sake of the relationship (as the story of Job illustrates) as well as for the completeness of the story and the spiritual directee's healing. A spiritual directee was sexually abused as a child. She was diagnosed and treated for PTSD by a psychotherapist. She still occasionally had distressing physical and emotional symptoms. She had remembered and learned many details of her traumatic experiences and believed her story was now complete. She was participating in a process to become a Catholic. She had a consistent prayer lite and was growing in ber relationship with God. Through her classes, prayer, and scripture, she believed that God was not to blame for what happened. In spiritual direction she asked, "But where was God? Where was God in my story?" The spiritual director suggested she stay with that question, keep praying about it, pose it directly to God, and avait for God's response. She did so for several weeks. Subsequently she described a vivid dream that held ber attention. The dream :vas not threaten- ing,-. in fast, the spiritual directee found it comforting, so she and the spiritual director explored it together. The spiritual director was drawn to this part and asked, "What was your grandmother's name?" The spiritual directee did not know. She continued to sense that the dream was very significant and prayed about it. In the next session the spiritual directee related that she had remained very comforted by the dream. She had learned from her mother that her grandmother s name was "Grave. "At the moment of hearing that, she felt '.flooded with consolation» that lasted a long cime. As she prayed about her reaction, her convic- tion grew that God had given ber the grace to survive ber trauma and was witb ber throughout ber experience. With this realization came healing. There was a noticeable shift in how she told her story and described herself She grew more confident that God would answer her prayers. Finding God in the Story In this example, a third stage of accompanying the spiritual directee with PTSD emerged: finding God in the story. The spiritual directee raised the question chat defines this stage. Some of life's deepest questions tome to the fore via trauma and the effort to find meaning in one's experience. This spiritual directee was firmly on a spiritual path and learning about a faith tradition; rhese are helpful in the search for answers as well as in recovery from PTSD. There was already movement toward God in her decision to not blame God for what happened. The process of reinembering the details and constructing the story sometimes provides a glimpse of God's involvement and creates a desire to learn more. Spiritual direction engages the desire to know God in one's experiences and fosters the encounter with God. A strength of spiritual direction is the treasured freedom to explicitly and hon- estly explore God's presence and action in one's story. The spiritual director did not attempt to answer the spiritual directee's faith question but cacher supported her interaction with God in her questioning. By encouraging her to pose her question to God, the spiritual director also supported God's desire for her freedom and her inti - mas with God. Through encouragement, the spiritual director's own confidence chat God was present in the spiritual directee's story was implied. The spiritual direc- tor trusted in God's intimate knowledge of the spiritual directee's experience and desire to bring the awareness and healing she needed. In this example the spiritual director made a decision to process the recalled dream of a spiritual directee. The dream was not the threatening, disturbing, recurring nightmare typical of PTSD. Instead, the spiritual directee reacted quise positively to the dream and desired to explore it. It seemed to be an ordinary dream char arose to address her actual life concern of answering a question about the trauma. The willingness of the spiritual direc- tor to help with the dream not only validated the spiritual directee's sense of its ' significance but also supported her relating to God in her story. A sense of mystery surrounded the spiritual director's inquiry about the grandmother's name; there was already a grace at work. The dream continued to be compelling to the spiritual directee; she stayed with what provid ed spiritual value. As it turned out, the spiritual directee saw her grandmother and her grandmother's name as powerful symbols of God's presence. More happened chan could have been expected by simply learning a fact. The word grace was not about information; it was about meaning. The spiritual directee encountered God and recognized grace in her story. Consolation flowed from God's involvement and manifested as enlightened under- standing. The spiritual directee became aware chat she was sustained and accompanied by God. The awareness was freeing, healing, and transforming. With the spiritual director as witness, she retold her story as the story of God present in her experience. The story became real for her, and her confidence and faith in God grew. She began to know herself in a new way, as someone accompanied by God. Her story was no longer only a human story. It was a story chat revisited an old horror and interpreted it in a new way. Remembrante is about the draina of God's love for us, and the spiritual directee's story pointed beyond itself to the larger, communal remembrante. Narrative as a sequence of events does not have the saure healing power as narrative to which we have assigned deep meaning and a connection to a larger story. In this example we see the challenge many spiritual directees face in reconciling beliefs about God's goodness and love with the reality of evil traumatically and person- ally experienced. Experience and beliefs seem to contra- dict one another. Old belief systems proue inadequate for the questions chat arise. Many theologians grapple with issues of gond and evil, but spiritual directees mat' not Volume 16 No. 4 • December 2010 1 1 SPIRITUAL DIRECTION find the intellectuel speculation all that helpful or con- vincing. Spiritual directors can simply encourage open - ness to God without in any way denying or minimizing the evil in what happened to the spiritual directee or feel- ing compelled to defend God. God handles God's own defense by acting with overwhelming goodness. Such inner experiences bring new convictions. Sometimes old belief systems are inadequate to contain new insights of God in one's story and experiences of God's goodness and profoundly healing touch. A spiritual directee was traumatized by abuse experienced as a youngster. He had done much self-work in psychotherapy and spiritual direction and had only occasional symptoms of PTSD, such as panic attacks and avoidingpersons and situ- ations that reminded him of bis trauma. He was also trou-bled by aféeling ofsomething "heavy» within that "blocked" him in relationships. He typically located the heaviness in an arec of the body where many person carry grief He worked in a Christian ministry setting and regularly practiced centering prayer. He preferred to pray with feminine images of God, although masculine images, particularly of Jesus, pervaded bis work. One dey in spiritual direction he described an experience in prayer ofa profound sense ofa shift within. The spiritual director asked him to say more. He recalled detaits and became energized as he reentered his experience. The spiritual director asked about feelings he was experiencing. He described "lightness » and "opening, » saying that something heavy had been removed. Eventually he connected his prayer experience with the rock being rolled away from Jesus' tomb. The spiritual director encouraged him to savor that image and to pray with it. The spiritual director also invited prayer with scriptures describing the relevant events in Jesus' life. Subsequently the spiritual directee described a deeper healing and freedom than he had thought possible. He reported greater confidence in the presence of the resurrected Christ in bis life. Weeks later he described another prayer experience in which another powerful "shift" within had occurred. Again he was encouraged to say more. This cime he reported an even greater sense of "incredible light" as the shift occurred and afierward "truly feeling the Spirit within, " more so than outside, himsee.' He expressed vert' positive emotions, including feelings of freedom and energy. He said that the heaviness within was gons. He said, 1 haven't really been much of a Jesus person before, but now 1 get him! This is new for me and it's exciting. " Developing and Revising the Belief System In spiritual direction we are accompanied in compas- sionate hope as we live with inadequate answers to our deep questions and cope with our wounds. We can freely reveal and verbalize our struggles with faith. Yet spiritual direction is also a place to dwell in the excitement of new energy and new beliefs as old grief and wounds are transformed through profound encounters with God. As healing of PTSD occurs, spiritual directees develop new and more adequate belief systems to make sense of their revised scories and tc, hold their experiences of transcen- dence and transformation. This is the fourth stage of journeying with spiritual directees with PTSD: develop- ing and revising the belief system. The spiritual directee in this exemple articulated a profound spiritual experience that transformed his heavy wound. He noticed a deep inner change. The spiritual director used the "evocative" approach described by Conroy (81 -82), helping the spiritual directee to stay with an important experience and "contemplate» it, remaining absorbed in what God revealed. The spiri- tual director elicited details, feelings, and images. As the spiritual directee savored and relived the experience, he described it in greater detail and felt energized. He named his feelings. Then he made a new convection. The "shift" was as if the rock rolled from jesus' tomb. The revelation he received was the presence of the resurrected Christ in his life. The spiritual director continuel to encourage savoring and praying about the experience and also recommended scripture. An ever-richer experience later occurred, in which even more light, healing, and freedom came into the spiritual directee's inner being. The spiritual director again used an evocative approach. The spiritual directee's contemplation led him to recog- nize God's touch even more deeply. The particular revela- tion for him was unity, which he expressed as incarnation and participation in jesus' resurrection. For the Christian spiritual directee, solidariry with Jesus' experiences and praying with the relevant scriptures 12 Presence: An International Journal of Spiritual Direction SPIRITUAL DIRECTION can be very fruitful and lead to deeper belief. Here, the persona] and direct encounter with the Divine and the healing it brought led to confirmation and broadening of belief Profound experiences like these are poten - tially more powerful chan the experience of trauma. The spiritual directee solidified his Christian "cake" on his experience; Jesus became a reality for him. The trans - formation the spiritual directee exp erienced was just what Christiane hope for in their remembrante of jesus, whose own trauma was not the last word. The mystery of resurrection from trauma was manifest in the spiritual directee's own experience. He gained a new sense of who he is, an incarnation of God. Once again, the individual's story connected to the larger story in the faith tradition. Summary PTSD affects up to two-thirds of persons who experi- ence or witness trauma. About hall the people who use outpatient mental health services have it. PTSD can cake a very long rime to resolve. Because of this incidence and longevity, many spiritual directors are likely to companion spiritual directees who have PTSD, whether diagnosed or not. Often the spiritual directee will be in or have had psychotherapy. It is possible to recover from PTSD, or at least for the symptoms to diminish. Spiritual directors can therefore be hopeful for these spiritual directees, espccially because persons firmly grounded in religions or spiritual paths tend to be more successful in healing. Understanding PTSD and the stages of healing and having confidence in God's desire to heal will help the spiritual director be a steady companion in the dif- ficult and lengthy process. The process includes much iteration, with each stage recurring again and again, requiring enormous energy, resilience, hope, and courage on the part of the spiritual directee and great patience, understanding, and compas- sion on the part of the spiritual d irector. These are all graces to be prayed for on the journey together. The spiri- tual directee may not be aware of or narre these stages but will experience their fruitfulness and find the terrain familiar as it is repeatedly encountered. As safety with the spiritual director is established, a trusting and hopeful partnership in healing gels underway. The spiritual direc- tor promotes integration by helping the spiritual directee bring the PTSD experiences into conversation with God, who will bring gond out of the very worst of experiences. The spiritual director listens and supports the construc- tion and the telling and retelling of difficult scories. Both spiritual director and spiritual directee trust and pray that God will be found in the story and th at the story will connect to the community's story of God -with-us. The spiritual director keeps faith with the spiritual directee as experiences of evil raire contradictions to beliefs. At cimes the spiritual director urges and shares in the contempla- tion of wonder and transformation and rejoices with the spiritual directee as freedom grows and belief and witness to Mystery strengthen. And then, for the spiritual direc- tor, there is gratitude for the privilege of participating in the work of God. M, Notes 1.
